name: Foot orthotic insoles

lead: Orthotic insoles are removable supports for the shoe, either custom made from a foot scan or bought ready made. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief and, in some products, extra height of a small amount, with people hoping for steadier standing and a more upright stance.

They redistribute load across the foot and may hold the arch or heel in a set position, and heel inserts raise the heel a little. Their best-studied use is heel pain from plantar fasciitis; no studies were found of them for posture, gait appearance or height in people without a foot problem.

paras: People slip them into everyday or athletic shoes, either a ready-made pair or a custom pair made from a cast or scan. Height-oriented inserts are worn like lifts inside the shoe and need enough shoe room to fit.

Reviews describe mixed evidence for medical use and inconsistent fit across methods. No harms of insoles themselves were identified in the sources reviewed; clinicians treat underlying foot conditions with several measures, not insoles alone.

angle.text: Some insoles add measurable height while worn, and others are used for comfort and arch support that people hope will help their stance. Trials have studied them for heel pain; effects on posture and looks have not been tested.

lead: Foot orthotic insoles, also called shoe inserts, foot orthoses or orthotics, are removable supports placed inside footwear. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief, orthopaedic correction, athletic performance and, in some products, added height. [1]

They are either custom made from a cast or scan of the foot or bought ready made. Medical uses are the best studied, notably heel pain from plantar fasciitis, where reviews list orthotics among first-line conservative measures. [1][2] Evidence for medical use is described as mixed, and no studies were found of insoles as a posture, gait-appearance or height tool in people without a foot condition. [1]
infobox: Custom-fabricated or prefabricated; firm, flexible or soft [1]
Foam, EVA, silicone gel, carbon fibre, leather [1]
Plantar fasciitis, arch and alignment problems, pressure relief [1][2]
Medical orthoses are prescribed by clinicians; ready-made insoles are sold over the counter

paras: Custom inserts are made by an orthotics laboratory from a plaster cast, foam impression or 3D scan, with digital scans used to drive CNC machines. Firm supports hold a fixed position, flexible supports move with the foot while supporting the arch, and soft supports of foam, gel or similar materials mainly absorb shock. Ready-made pads and heel inserts are also sold. Wikipedia reports that none of the three fitting methods produces a proper fit more than about 80 percent of the time. [1]

Orthotics as a field is broader than insoles and includes ankle-foot orthoses and braces for other body regions. Grokipedia describes the history of the field, from ancient splints to the plastics of the 1960s and 3D printing, but that history concerns orthotics generally rather than insoles. [3]

A review in American Family Physician describes plantar fasciitis as a self-limiting cause of heel pain with excessive foot pronation as a risk factor. [2] A 2025 Danish review states that first-line treatment is conservative, including unloading, stretching, eccentric exercise, suitable footwear and orthotics, with about 90 percent of patients improving within a year.  A Cureus review of diagnosis and management frameworks covers the same condition. [4]

A paediatric review says flatfoot in children is usually a benign variant and that treatment is indicated for symptomatic cases.  Reviews of Morton's neuroma list orthotics among treatment options. [5] Wikipedia says medical use is criticised for weak evidence, that podiatrists often prescribe different orthoses for the same patient, and that patients often report short-term comfort gains. [1]

A randomised trial of 48 patients with plantar fasciitis gave all participants shoe inserts and compared plantar-specific stretching with high-load strength training, with the strength group faring better at follow-up. This tested exercise, not the inserts themselves.  A pragmatic randomised equivalence trial compared heel lifts with calf eccentric exercise for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. [6] A randomised trial examined different foot orthoses and gait mechanics in people with rheumatoid arthritis. [7]
No published trials were found of insoles used for height, posture or appearance in healthy people.

Wikipedia lists height enhancement among the reasons for which shoe inserts are sold. [1] No community material about insoles was available for this entry, so how forums discuss them is not documented here.
